articles.title: Peter Chan Rules Out AI-Generated Content, Says Feature Films Will Survive the Rise of Vertical Dramas
articles.summary: Acclaimed Asian filmmaker Peter Chan Ho-sun, director of “Comrades: Almost a Love Story” and “The Warlords,” said he will probably use AI in his filmmaking but “definitely not AIGC,” or AI-generated content, and that the two-hour feature will hold its ground against short-form and vertical dramas…
body: Young audiences’ shrinking attention spans have them turning to short and vertical dramas, Chan said, while at the other end, people are listening to podcasts that run for hours, and Christopher Nolan did podcasts around the world to explain his purist approach of making “Oppenheimer” the way movies were made in the ’50s. “So there are two completely opposite ends of the spectrum that are surviving and thriving simultaneously. So I believe that movie will be around for a long, long time,” he told a rapt audience at the Grand Ballroom, Marina Bay Sands.

Chan’s latest film, “The Road Not Taken,” premiered in Toronto. “My new movie is about Alzheimer’s, but it’s really not just about Alzheimer’s. It’s about a broken family that has all sorts of problems a family could have,” he said.

articles.summary: The surly miser Ebenezer Scrooge is no longer just a fictional character haunting the holidays — he’s on Venmo. To promote Ti West’s upcoming adaptation of the notorious character in the film “Ebenezer,” starring Johnny Depp in the titular role, the Paramount promotional team created a Venmo…
body: Although Scrooge’s Venmo is dishing out money, he also appears to be accepting it. The public feed of his account is filled with payments made out to him. “For cheers and joy! (And maybe a little luck please)” one benefactor wrote. Another wrote, “$ Retainer Fee — for the Ghost of Christmas Past to haunt my exes with a little bah humbug spirit.” Several others paid Scrooge to boost his Christmas spirit.

Paramount Pictures’ “Ebenezer” will hit theaters on Nov. 13. The official logline reads: “The name you know, the story you don’t.” Judging from the trailer, West — known for directing the horror trilogy “X” — is zooming in on the darker aspects of Charles Dickens’ beloved story, showing Depp’s character being haunted by some seriously scary ghosts and getting buried alive.

Depp stars alongside Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Arthur Conti, Ellie Bamber, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Charlie Murphy, Tramell Tillman and Ian McKellen. Based on “A Christmas Carol” by Charles Dickens, Nathaniel Halpern adapted the screenplay.

articles.title: Michael Gray, Star of ‘Shazam!’ TV Series, Dies at 75
articles.summary: Michael Gray, the star of the 1970s “Shazam!” television series, died on Friday in Palm Desert from natural causes. He was 75. Gray first got his break in television in 1972 when he was cast in NBC’s “The Little People” alongside Brian Keith and Shelly Fabares.
body: “From my very first day on ‘Shazam!,’ Mike and Les [Tremayne] welcomed me like a king,” Davey said about Gray. “Mike was just a loving, sweet guy with a great sense of humor. He loved acting, loved doing the show and, in recent years, loved appearing at comic cons. He really enjoyed meeting and chatting with the fans. Mike was a wonderful man. I don’t think he ever stopped smiling.”

“Shazam!” was remastered in 2012 for distribution on DVD, which sparked a career resurgence for Gray. In recent years, he appeared in several episodes of the FX series “Archer” as one of the titular character’s boyhood idols, as well as appearing in “Surge of Power” on AMC’s “Comic Book Men.” When “Shazam! Fury of the Gods” released in 2023, Gray made a brief cameo where he interacted with Zachary Levi’s Captain Marvel as a nod to the original series.

articles.title: Nana Patekar obituary
articles.summary: Indian actor known for his roles in Salaam Bombay! and the Bollywood hits Parinda and Krantiveer, who had a controversial personal life. The Indian actor Nana Patekar, who has died of a heart attack aged 75, first broke through in Mira Nair’s Salaam Bombay!
body: Until that point, Patekar’s rougher edges had mostly been celebrated. As an actor, he demonstrated a baggy-eyed naturalism that spoke more to Bombay streetlife than Bollywood fantasy. He was given to writing out his dialogue until he had internalised it, and his growling line readings were both idiosyncratic and much imitated. Satyajit Ray counted among the actor’s most illustrious admirers, but apparently could not find a suitable project for him; Patekar instead had Nair to thank for launching him to international prominence in Salaam Bombay! as Baba Golub, the brutal pimp and drug dealer lording over an army of street children.

articles.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
articles.summary: Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave in 2021.
body: A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.
Trump cancelled a previous deposition - or interview under oath - on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance".
But a lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia that day and had "prioritised that" over answering the questions.
President Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is in the phase known as "discovery", where the two sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence.

articles.title: Republican leader embarrassed by Ali G film says he plans to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’
articles.summary: Exclusive: Michael Aboud, whose actions in what he believed to be a documentary are likely to come under considerable scrutiny, has expressed anger at the film-maker. • This article contains substantial spoilers for Ali G: Who Iz I? • Review: Ali G: Who Iz I?
body: The chair of the El Paso County Republican Party has said he intends to sue Sacha Baron Cohen over footage of the local politician used in new satirical comedy Ali G: Who Iz I?

In the film, Michael Aboud is shown taking part in a training programme with another Cohen character, ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad, who instructs Aboud and fellow Maga sympathisers in self-defence techniques including the wearing, over clothes, of protective plastic buttocks. He also schools them in how to fire bullets from the middle of these buttocks by the repeated up and down manipulation of a rubber penis.

Aboud and a fellow student, former preacher and aspirant actor Joshua Loudermilk, are then recruited by Morad to help in a mission to prevent the birth in the US of the baby of a (fictional) South American drugs kingpin.

This involves Aboud and Loudermilk abducting his heavily-pregnant girlfriend and driving her in a phoney ambulance to a remote unstaffed medical facility, where she gives birth (to a lifelike prosthetic).

articles.title: Ali G: Who Iz I? review – Sacha Baron Cohen’s high-stakes satire punches up and down with spectacular bad taste
articles.summary: Baron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generation. • Exclusive: Republican leader embarrassed by film says he plays to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’ If you liked Sacha Baron…
body: I f you liked Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G the first time around, you’ll like this less; if you disliked it, you’ll dislike this more; if you suspected it was racist, you’ll be more emboldened to say so – especially as Baron Cohen has dreamed up a whole new character apparently to pre-empt and mock precisely that objection. Broad and crass as it often is – in fact always is – this Ali G sequel is sometimes funny: the athletic vigour of our hero’s pranking and punking is like the umpteenth Jackass film at which you might find yourself laughing, and Baron Cohen blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed.

The insurmountable problem is that the film keeps having to tell you who is and isn’t “in on it”: at the beginning, over the closing credits at the end and even briefly in the middle of the action. Well, Ali G was from so very long ago, and even the high-water mark of Baron Cohen’s Borat popularity was quite long ago, and the online media scene now so fragmented that … yes … people have forgotten, a whole new generation doesn’t know. People really don’t recognise him.
points: Baron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generation.

articles.title: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope
articles.summary: The pop star beat artists like Paul McCartney, Suede and Jade Thirlwall to lift the £25,000 prize.
body: Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope.
A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood glamour, it beat the likes of Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Jade to scoop the £25,000 prize.
"I couldn't tell you how grateful I am to be holding this," said Raye, clutching her trophy at Newcastle's Utilita Arena. "I'm shaking, I'm jet-lagged, I'm tired. It's all blurry."
It is the first time a pop album has won the coveted prize - which recognises the best British or Irish album of the last 12 months - since M People's Elegant Slumming in 1994.

articles.title: Tom Skerritt, Alien and Top Gun actor, dies aged 93
articles.summary: Actor also had roles in M*A*S*H, A River Runs Through It and Picket Fences in career spanning 60 years. Tom Skerritt, the actor known for roles in Alien and Top Gun, has died at the age of 93. His publicist confirmed to Variety that he died from natural causes.
body: “While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives,” a family statement shared with People read.
In a career spanning more than 60 years, the actor had more than 170 big and small screen credits, winning an Emmy and receiving Golden Globe and Screen Actors Guild award nominations.

After serving a four-year tour of duty in the US air force, Skerritt made his big-screen debut in the 1962 war film War Hunt alongside Robert Redford and Sydney Pollack, but his breakout came in 1970 with a role in Robert Altman’s hit satire M*A*S*H. The film was a major box office hit and was nominated for the best picture Oscar.

The 1970s saw Skerritt follow the film with roles in the cult black comedy Harold and Maude, Altman’s crime drama Thieves Like Us, Roger Corman’s sexploitation comedy Big Bad Mama and the Oscar-nominated ballet drama The Turning Point.
points: Actor also had roles in M*A*S*H, A River Runs Through It and Picket Fences in career spanning 60 years.

articles.title: Seeking Truth: Tom Skerritt (1933-2026)
articles.summary: Like all great storytellers, Tom Skerritt was an observer. He loved to tell you that he learned about acting and filmmaking on the job, lucky enough to stand alongside masters like Robert Altman and Ridley Scott early in his career, absorbing everything he could about the art of moviemaking.
body: Skerritt gave a few fun performances in the ‘80s like “SpaceCamp” and “Steel Magnolias,” but it was his turn as CDR “Viper” Metcalf in “Top Gun” that again shot him into the pop culture stratosphere. His most underrated run as a performer might come in the ‘90s, when he made “A River Runs Through It,” “Singles,” and “Contact,” consecutively. The big break chronologically between those last two was taken up by “Picket Fences,” a huge hit for CBS that won Skerritt an Emmy. He never stopped popping up on TV shows and was a part of the legacy of “Cheers,” “Roseanne,” “Will & Grace,” and “The West Wing.”

Film roles became more sporadic in his old age, but he loved working into his eighties, including a memorable role in the excellent “Lucky,” his last great turn, and a fitting epitaph to his career. So many incredible people in that movie are gone now: Stanton, David Lynch, and Skerritt. But the work remains.

Watch the clip below and experience these two lost legends finding so much truth in such a simple interaction. There’s a line that Stanton’s Lucky says in the film: “The truth of the universe is waiting.” Tom Skerritt didn’t wait; he found that truth in everything he did.
